chapter.name: Forest and Wildlife Resources
chapter.blurb: Biodiversity and why forests are primary producers in India's ecological system; the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the species it named; Project Tiger; the Reserved/Protected/Unclassed classification of forest land and its state-wise spread; and community, traditional and religious conservation practices including Joint Forest Management and Sacred Groves.

scope_in.item: Explain what biodiversity means and why forests are described as the key primary producers in India's ecological system
State that India is one of the world's richest countries in biological diversity, with possibly twice or thrice the number of species yet to be discovered
Describe why conservation of forest and wildlife is necessary and what it preserves: ecological diversity, life-support systems (water, air, soil), and genetic diversity of plants and animals
State the year and key provisions of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act and name the animal species it specifically protected, including the later additions of 1980, 1986 and 1991
Describe Project Tiger: the tiger population figures of 1973, the threats to tigers, the launch year, and name India's tiger reserves and the states they are in
Explain the three government forest categories -- Reserved, Protected and Unclassed Forests -- and describe their state-wise distribution pattern
Describe community-led conservation efforts: the Sariska mining protest, the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri' in Alwar, the Chipko movement, Beej Bachao Andolan, Navdanya and Joint Forest Management
Describe Sacred Groves and religiously-motivated conservation practices, including the trees and animals named as sacred by different communities
Use the chapter's two newspaper extracts (on the gharial's decline and on the Yamuna bird deaths) as examples of ongoing threats to wildlife

concepts.name: Biodiversity and Flora and Fauna in India
concepts.description: What biodiversity means, why forests are the ecological system's primary producers, and why India's rich flora and fauna are nonetheless under stress.
concepts.idea: Biodiversity is the immense variety of life sharing the planet with us, and forests are the key primary producers that keep this entire ecological web alive.
concepts.rule: Biodiversity or Biological Diversity is immensely rich in wildlife and cultivated species, diverse in form and function but closely integrated in a system through multiple network of interdependencies. Humans, along with all living organisms, form a complex web of an ecological system in which humans are only a part and are very much dependent on this system for their own existence; forests are primary producers on which all other living beings depend. India is one of the world's richest countries in terms of its vast array of biological diversity, possibly twice or thrice the number of species yet to be discovered. Diverse flora and fauna are so well integrated in daily life that they are taken for granted, and are under great stress mainly due to insensitivity to our environment.
concepts.example: Plants, animals and micro-organisms re-create the quality of the air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that produces our food, without which we cannot survive.

concepts.name: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and conservation of threatened species
concepts.description: Why conservation was needed, the 1972 Act's provisions, the named species it protected, and how the protected list widened in 1980, 1986 and 1991.
concepts.idea: The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 gave the country's first organised legal shield to endangered species and their habitats, and its coverage has widened over time from a handful of large animals to insects and plants.
concepts.rule: The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act was implemented in 1972, with provisions for protecting habitats, an all-India list of protected species, banning hunting, and restricting trade in wildlife. It focused on protecting specific gravely-threatened animals: the tiger, the one-horned rhinoceros, the Kashmir stag or hangul, three types of crocodiles (fresh water crocodile, saltwater crocodile and the Gharial), and the Asiatic lion; more recently the Indian elephant, black buck (chinkara), the great Indian bustard (godawan) and the snow leopard have been given full or partial legal protection. Under notifications of 1980 and 1986, several hundred butterflies, moths, beetles and one dragonfly were added to the protected list; in 1991, plants were added for the first time, starting with six species.
concepts.example: Fisheries are heavily dependent on the maintenance of aquatic biodiversity, which is one reason conservation preserves genetic diversity for better growth and breeding of species.

concepts.name: Project Tiger
concepts.description: The collapse of the tiger population by 1973, the threats behind it, the launch of Project Tiger, and India's named tiger reserves.
concepts.idea: Project Tiger, launched in 1973, is India's best-known species-specific conservation campaign, begun after the tiger population was found to have collapsed from about 55,000 to 1,827.
concepts.rule: In 1973 the authorities realised the tiger population had dwindled to 1,827 from an estimated 55,000 at the turn of the century, due to threats such as poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey base species and growing human population. Since India and Nepal provide habitat to about two-thirds of the world's surviving tiger population, these two nations became prime targets for poaching and illegal trading. Project Tiger was launched in 1973. Some of India's tiger reserves are Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand), Sunderbans National Park (West Bengal), Bandhavgarh National Park (Madhya Pradesh), Sariska Wildlife Sanctuary (Rajasthan), Manas Tiger Reserve (Assam) and Periyar Tiger Reserve (Kerala).
concepts.example: The trade of tiger skins and the use of tiger bones in traditional medicines, especially in Asian countries, left the tiger population on the verge of extinction, which is why Project Tiger was launched in 1973.

concepts.name: Types and distribution of forest resources
concepts.description: The Reserved, Protected and Unclassed Forest categories the government uses to classify forest land, and how their shares differ from state to state.
concepts.idea: India's forest and wildlife resources are classified by ownership and protection status into Reserved, Protected and Unclassed Forests, and the mix of these three varies sharply from state to state.
concepts.rule: Reserved Forests (more than half of total forest land) are regarded as the most valuable for conservation of forest and wildlife resources. Protected Forests (almost one-third of total forest area) are protected from any further depletion. Unclassed Forests are other forests and wastelands belonging to both government and private individuals and communities. Reserved and Protected Forests together are called permanent forest estates, maintained for producing timber and other forest produce and for protective reasons. Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests (75 per cent of its total forest area); Jammu and Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Maharashtra have large percentages of reserved forests; Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan have a bulk of protected forests; all North-Eastern states and parts of Gujarat have a very high percentage of unclassed forests managed by local communities.
concepts.example: Because Reserved and Protected Forests are maintained for producing timber and other forest produce as well as for protective reasons, they are together referred to as permanent forest estates.

questions.a: Not necessarily. 'Most valuable for conservation' describes how Reserved Forests are officially regarded and formally protected by the Forest Department, which the chapter presents as a status or classification. The chapter does not state that Unclassed Forests, despite lacking this formal status, are poorly protected -- in the North-East and parts of Gujarat, they are managed by local communities, and elsewhere the chapter shows community-led conservation, such as the Chipko movement or Sacred Groves, being highly effective even without formal Reserved status. So the chapter gives no basis to conclude that formal classification and actual on-the-ground protection always match.

concepts.name: Community, traditional and religious conservation practices
concepts.description: How local communities protect forests and wildlife through direct action, Joint Forest Management, and traditional or religious reverence such as Sacred Groves.
concepts.idea: Across India, local and tribal communities protect forests and wildlife through direct action, traditional farming and religious reverence, often without waiting for or even accepting government involvement.
concepts.rule: In Sariska Tiger Reserve, Rajasthan, villagers fought mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act; five villages in the Alwar district declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', banning hunting under their own rules. The Chipko movement in the Himalayas resisted deforestation and proved community afforestation successful. The Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya showed diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is viable. Joint Forest Management (JFM) has existed formally since 1988, when Odisha passed the first resolution; it forms local village institutions that protect degraded forest land in return for non-timber forest produce and a share of harvested timber. Sacred Groves are virgin forest patches preserved by tribal nature worship, left untouched; the Mundas and Santhal of Chota Nagpur worship mahua and kadamba trees, and tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship tamarind and mango trees during weddings. In Bishnoi villages of Rajasthan, blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks are protected as part of the community.
concepts.example: The inhabitants of five villages in the Alwar district of Rajasthan declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', setting their own rules that ban hunting and protect wildlife against outside encroachment.

questions.a: The examples show that community-led conservation can work well in specific, local cases -- villagers in Sariska stopping mining by citing the law, five Alwar villages setting and enforcing their own no-hunting rules over 1,200 hectares, or the Chipko movement resisting deforestation and successfully afforesting land.
